sources.locator: Sections 'Big Time, Small Town' (wrestling, coach anecdote, father's MS, brother and the army), 'Flair for the Dramatic' (coupon sales, Denver office, Maui, Henry), 'The Outsider' (Rae Dawn Chong, Moneyball, Zero Dark Thirty, Guardians audition). sources.excerpt: “I’d be devastated,” he said. “Because I put everything into it … “I was like, ‘I don’t know, but I know I’ll be famous and I know I’ll make a shit ton of money.’ ” … a salesman only has one product: himself. “I was great at that,” … I had everyone convinced I’d been off doing this great sales job and making money, and I wasn’t. I had no prospects, no job, was still sort of riding the glory of high school. … ‘I’m more in debt every month. I’m so depressed. I can’t do it.’ … My friends picked me up in a van. They had a cooler of beer. But I was not in a great place. … He said, ‘Jesus told me to talk to you . . .’ At that moment I was like, I think I have to go with this guy. … He says, “Fuck, yeah, I act. Put me in a movie.” … That was the first time I heard someone say, ‘We’re not gonna cast you—you’re too fat.’ So I decided to drop the weight, like in wrestling. … You walk into the room as the character. You let them think the person you are is close to the character they want. You make them think you already are that guy. … He ended up going into the army and told me not to. I think he saw something in me. I was a peculiar kid. … There’s going to be a point in life where you’re going to have to prove that your family is more important to you than show business. … he was a hard man to connect with. … sees it as divinely ordained … That's why I believe in God and the divine … I feel like it was perfectly planned. … That was the carrot Pratt was chasing. It took 15 months, but he finally got it. … One of my best friends heard I'd been floundering. … I was always giving away my shifts because I didn't have much overhead. … It was supposed to be a one-episode deal, a guest spot, but the character took off. Pratt gained weight while shooting the first season—partly because he thought it worked for the character, partly because he'd just been married … If left untreated, it can be devastating, and he left it untreated. … I was very much an individual and happy to be an individual. I dressed funny and was comfortable in my own skin. … I played the room.
sources.context: Long-form cover profile reported while Pratt cooked at his home during a self-declared work break after Guardians of the Galaxy, Jurassic World and Passengers. The high-school coach exchange is Vanity Fair relaying an Entertainment Weekly interview (the EW original refused automated access and was not opened). The Rae Dawn Chong dialogue is Cohen's reconstruction from Pratt's telling. 'A salesman only has one product: himself' is Cohen's paraphrase of Pratt; 'I was great at that' is Pratt's direct quote. The Jim Carrey line is Carrey's advice as Pratt relayed it. The dek ('he sees it as divinely ordained') is Vanity Fair's framing. 'He left it untreated' is Pratt's account of his father's multiple sclerosis, not independent medical record.

Edit stage (2026-10-29) reopened a fuller copy of the same GQ page (the jury's curl copies) that includes the 'happy plump man' paragraph (Pratt: 'first guy in line to buy that line of bullshit', 'I also understood that there was value to it', the Chris Farley comparison and 'I think that's often the case with comedians'), the 'crybaby' childhood answer, the 'cerebral person' passage before Gunn's remarks, and the Delivery Man paragraph (295 pounds).
sources.excerpt: No one being like a super-confident dumb fat guy.’ So I started. … ’Oh great, I found my niche—this is paying better than the asshole-boyfriend parts.’ … I think I was outwardly having more fun. I was more fun to be around, probably. That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more. … Obnoxious. I was obnoxious, really hyperactive, disruptive...but also Dad was very, very strict, so if I got yelled at, I would stay silent for a long period of time. I was really sensitive. That's fascinating to people. … Why is this guy not crippled with self-doubt? … I don't think Chris Farley did feel that way. … to hide the fact that he didn't feel what he was projecting on the outside. I think that's often the case with comedians. … the highlights of his days were the eating and drinking but that the rest wasn't so good, that he felt physically and mentally sluggish and "didn't feel too great about who I was." … My bones ached, I had cardiovascular issues, I was unhealthy, I was feeling rotten. … I was really sensitive. I cried a lot. I was a crybaby for a long time. … I'm a much more cerebral person than you may expect. … really I'm thinking a lot, in my head below the surface. … Delivery Man, the 2013 Vince Vaughn movie in which Pratt bulked up to 295 pounds for a supporting role
sources.context: Jurassic World-era cover profile. The 'image that I was casting' line answers Heath's question about why Anna Faris may have preferred him heavier; Pratt was joking in part ('I was like a great pet fat guy'). Gunn's remarks describe the first half of the Guardians of the Galaxy shoot, when Pratt overthought his choices. The 'stupid director' line is about early films where his ad-libs were cut and then used. The 'image that I was casting' answer comes directly after Pratt describes the heavy years as physically and emotionally bad ('feeling rotten', 'didn't feel too great about who I was') and compares his cheerful persona to Chris Farley's; it concerns his own offscreen self and interview persona, not the Andy Dwyer character. The 'cerebral person' line is framed by Pratt as what Gunn would say ('I wouldn't want to be quoted [sounding like I was] saying this about myself').

sources.context: Cover story reported in Atlanta during Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 filming, timed to Jurassic World Dominion and The Terminal List. Rapkin says the conversation turned to the online backlash 'at his prompting'. The Elliot Page statement text is the 2019 statement as Men's Health quotes it (the original Instagram post was not opened). The Zoe Church film detail is Men's Health's reporting about pastor Chad Veach, not Pratt's statement. 'I cried about it' refers to coverage of an Instagram post about his wife that Pratt feared his son Jack, then nine, would read. The backlash conversation began 'at his prompting'. The tears were over articles reading his 'healthy daughter' Instagram post as a dig at Faris and their premature son, not over faith coverage. Gunn's 'about his politics' remark and the writer's box-office aside are offered as other causes of the online hostility. Attribution: the box-office line is the writer Mickey Rapkin's own aside to Pratt, and Gunn's 'literally just made up' remark was given to Rapkin. Neither appears in the Daily Beast's response (checked against the full Daily Beast text at verify and repair).

I mean, I do the animated movies, which are fun … I've been playing this Terminal List character James Reese and then I've been doing some other things, Mercy I did recently … more of a seriousness in some of the roles … I kind of kicked in my door to door sales skills right there
sources.context: Long-form, faith-forward conversation; co-host Ben Sasse has terminal cancer, and Pratt ends by interviewing him. Pratt is the speaker in every quoted passage, identified by first-person biography (Virginia, Minnesota; the Denver office; his father's MS; 'married to... Anna, to Jack's mom'; his manager). A later Sasse remark about his own salesman father is not Pratt's. Two machine transcriptions, not a human listen; the models differ only on filler and spelling ('towny'/'townie'), which should not be quoted. The marketplace passage answers a host question about how he navigated the reaction to his 2018 MTV speech (he notes his first date with Katherine was the next day), so 'up until that point' refers to the years before that speech. In the comedy-plan answer he names his recent roles' seriousness, comedy as 'something I have' and working close to home; he names Mercy as a recent role ('Mercy I did recently') without discussing its reception, and he says he means live-action roles because he already does animated films.

claims.claim: Metadata description summarizing Pratt's 2015 GQ answer: the happy fat guy of his Parks years was an image cast to convince people he was okay.
claims.passage: Chris Pratt says the happy fat guy of his Parks and Rec years was an image he cast to convince people he was okay.
claims.inference: Accurate paraphrase of the GQ answer about his own offscreen persona in the heavy years (not the Andy character).
claims.alternative: The line was partly joking and sat inside an answer about feeling unhealthy; the body quotes the surrounding context.

claims.claim: Asked by GQ whether he discussed his weight with Anna Faris, Pratt said she was "so okay with it" and "Probably in many ways preferred me that way."
claims.passage: He said his wife at the time, Anna Faris, had been "so okay with it" and had probably preferred him heavier.
claims.inference: Sets up the question his "image" answer responds to.
claims.alternative: It is his guess about her preference, not her statement.

claims.claim: In 2015 Pratt told GQ that in his heavy years 'My bones ached, I had cardiovascular issues, I was unhealthy, I was feeling rotten.'
claims.passage: My bones ached, I had cardiovascular issues, I was unhealthy, I was feeling rotten.
claims.inference: Restores the health context of the hook answer: the heavy years felt bad underneath.
claims.alternative: Health alone can explain the later change in his habits without any image motive.

claims.claim: Asked why Anna Faris may have preferred him heavier, Pratt said: 'I think I was outwardly having more fun... That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more.'
claims.passage: That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more.
claims.inference: In context (GQ 2015) the 'image' is his own offscreen and interview persona during the heavy Parks years, not Andy's happiness. The answer follows his account of feeling 'rotten' and 'didn't feel too great about who I was', his Farley comparison and 'I also understood that there was value to it'. Read with those lines, the front covered a self-worth problem and had market value, which supports 3 only in combination with c-value. 'Now I have less fun. I focus more' belongs to this health and self-regard answer, not to the Moneyball story (VF 2017). Limit: one answer, partly joking.
claims.alternative: Pratt himself frames the persona as a mask over feelings that did not match it ('I think that's often the case with comedians'), which is the 7 pain-masking reading in his own words; health, not image, also explains 'less fun'.

claims.claim: GQ records that Pratt laughed and said "I was like a great pet fat guy" right after the image answer.
claims.passage: Then he laughed: "I was like a great pet fat guy."
claims.inference: Shows the answer was delivered partly as a joke.
claims.alternative: The joke may mean the whole answer should be weighted lightly.

claims.claim: GQ reports Pratt saying that during the heavy years he 'didn't feel too great about who I was.'
claims.passage: an image cast over a man who "didn't feel too great about who I was."
claims.inference: What sat under the cheerful front, in his account, was a self-regard problem. That is closer to a 3's worth/shame theme than to 7 fear or deprivation.
claims.alternative: Low self-regard during weight gain and heavy drinking is ordinary and not type-specific; GQ paraphrases most of the sentence and quotes only this phrase.

claims.claim: Pratt told GQ: 'I'm sure I was the first guy in line to buy that line of bullshit,' about the happy-plump-man persona of his comedy years.
claims.passage: I'm sure I was the first guy in line to buy that line of bullshit
claims.inference: He partly believed his own cheerful front; the image was not purely strategic.
claims.alternative: Self-deception about a mask fits the 7 reading as well as the 3 reading.

claims.claim: Pratt compared his persona to Chris Farley's, who in his view 'didn't feel what he was projecting on the outside'.
claims.passage: compared himself to Chris Farley, who in his view "didn't feel what he was projecting on the outside."
claims.inference: He frames the cheerful front as covering feelings that did not match it.
claims.alternative: This is the strongest first-person support for the 7 pain-masking reading.

claims.claim: Pratt told GQ: 'I also understood that there was value to it' about the happy-fat-guy persona.
claims.passage: Then he added: "I also understood that there was value to it."
claims.inference: In the same answer as the pain, he names the persona's market value: the front had a price he understood. This pairing of worth problem and market value is the 3 strand of the quote.
claims.alternative: Any working comic knows what gets laughs; 'value' may mean comic value rather than career value.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the GQ answer contains both a front over pain and a front with a price.
claims.passage: That answer holds both halves of the puzzle: a front over pain, and a front with a price.
claims.inference: Names the ambiguity the article then tests: pain (7) versus price/worth (3).
claims.alternative: The answer may be a single self-deprecating riff not meant to carry a motive.

claims.passage: he had been "kind of like the star of my hometown," and now "I just felt like super depressed."

type_hypothesis.against: Real counterevidence. The Maui year (about 2000) is the longest off-camera stretch in the record and fun beat ambition: he drank, smoked weed, worked 15 to 20 hours a week, was 'always giving away my shifts' (VF 2017) and called it 'a charming time' (2014). He describes a hyperactive, transgressive childhood (GQ 2015), and Gunn reports a new idea every day; both read 7. He frames his happy-fat-guy persona as a mask over feelings that didn't match it, like Chris Farley's ('I think that's often the case with comedians', GQ 2015), which is the 7 pain-masking reading in his own words. He remembers being 'a peculiar kid... comfortable in my own skin' (VF 2017). He tells his rise as providence and many pivotal moves came from others (mother, friend, Henry, brother, agent, manager), which reads 9 or 6; he calls himself 'too much of a people pleaser' and 'completely deferential'. Overt self-promotion needed a push (the photo, 2026). He broke his publicist's line to defend his son in 2022 and cried over coverage he feared Jack would read. He has kept public faith commitments since 2012, says he 'stood for something' and won't apologize (2026), and in 2026 called Hollywood an industry that creates 'idols to burn'. Most of the 3 evidence is self-report in interviews.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: His public persona is the classic 7: a hyperactive, disruptive, naked-on-the-bus jokester (GQ 2015) with real appetites, 'a new idea every day about everything' (Gunn), lapsed vows (Christian Post 2025), and a Maui year of partying and giving away shifts that he called 'a charming time'. His humor began as 'a self-defense mechanism' against a disapproving father (MH 2022), and he compared his cheerful fat-guy front to Chris Farley's, a mask over feelings that didn't match: 'I think that's often the case with comedians' (GQ 2015). On that reading 'to convince people that I was okay' is a 7 describing his own mask, and the reading is partly his.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What the cheerful front protects. A 7's front keeps pain, deprivation and limits out of the room; a 3's keeps failure out of sight and tracks what earns approval. Where Pratt's record reaches past the demands of acting, it points more often to worth and market value than to pain: after the sales collapse he 'had everyone convinced' he was succeeding while talking freely, later, about the depression (VF 2017; NDY 2026); explaining the happy fat guy he pairs the pain ('didn't feel too great about who I was') with its price ('I also understood that there was value to it'; 'paying better') (GQ 2015); and he describes his pre-2018 professional self as 'completely deferential to whatever the world wants... Just keep me employed as an actor' after 'I always sort of understood how I was seen in the marketplace' (NDY 2026, two transcription models). Versus 9: the deference carries a purpose clause (employment) and sits beside competitive selling ('I sold 500' vs 17 or 22) and a 15-month chase for the office. Limits: dieting and audition craft are professional incentives any actor shares; the hidden failure rests on one self-report; Faris's 2021 remark is weak, is not counted and is no longer cited; and the Maui year fits 7 better than 3, which the 3 reading answers only with an interpretation (a stalled young man who seized the first route back to success).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The 3 reading does not explain: the Maui year of drift and fun; his faith commitment, which he frames as the end of his deferential marketplace years and keeps public through criticism (though faith audiences are also a market and his framing shifts by outlet); his breaking the publicist's line to defend his son; his reluctance about overt self-promotion; his reliance on trusted advisers for big decisions (9 or 6); his stated wish for a smaller life ('work to live'; home above career by 2026); and his memory of himself as 'a peculiar kid... comfortable in my own skin'. Wing is left open.
